note: Links from this pack to candidates of the AI and biosecurity pack (branch ai-bio-pack, not admitted), pinned by sibling-ids.json. No record here re-states them. 'why' is Selekoa's orientation; 'siblingText' is the sibling record's own statement or the proposition's name, copied at the pinned commit.

links.siblingText: Biological design tools pose risks distinct from those of language models
links.why: The sibling pack's proposition B4: AI tools built to design or predict biological molecules or systems pose misuse risks distinct from language models. The models recorded in this pack (structure prediction, protein design, protein and genomic language models) are the kind of tool the proposition is about; this pack records no position on it.

links.siblingText: Sandbrink's preprint (arXiv v1, 24 June 2023) differentiates large language models from biological design tools, stating that language models in particular lower barriers to biological misuse while design tools expand the capabilities of sophisticated actors.
links.why: A text that articulates B4 (Sandbrink, arXiv v1, 24 June 2023).

links.siblingText: The preprint "Towards Responsible Governance of Biological Design Tools" (arXiv v1, 27 November 2023) states that biological design tools pose distinct regulatory challenges and that regulatory proposals tailored to large language models may be less effective for them.
links.why: A text that articulates B4 (preprint of 27 November 2023 on governance of biological design tools).

links.siblingText: CSET's explainer of December 2023 treats biological design tools as a separate class from chatbots, stating that their use in its current state requires both scientific and programming expertise.
links.why: A text that articulates B4 (CSET explainer, December 2023).

links.siblingText: Sandbrink's preprint (arXiv v1, 24 June 2023) states that biological design tools will expand the capabilities of sophisticated actors, and proposes interventions to deter biological misuse by such actors.
links.why: Sandbrink's statement that biological design tools will expand the capabilities of sophisticated actors (proposition B7).

links.siblingText: Synthesis-order screening is a control point for AI-related biological risk
links.why: The sibling pack's proposition B5 on synthesis-order screening as a control point.

links.siblingText: The preprint of 27 November 2023 states that the design capabilities of biological design tools could be used to evade DNA screening techniques, against the premise that screening at synthesis is a dependable control point.
links.why: A text that contests B5 on the ground that design tools could be used to evade screening; recorded at policy level in the sibling pack.

links.siblingText: Public release of model weights increases biological misuse risk
links.why: The sibling pack's proposition B6 on public release of model weights; several models in this pack were released with weights, as their papers or developers state.

links.siblingText: The preprint of 27 November 2023 identifies, among the challenges of regulating biological design tools, the potential for safeguards to be circumvented by open-sourcing model weights.
links.why: A text that names open-sourcing of model weights among the challenges of regulating biological design tools (B6).

links.siblingText: Working paper BWC/MSP/2025/WP.4, submitted by the United Kingdom to the 2025 Meeting of States Parties, states in its fifty-year timeline of life-science advances that the AlphaFold protein-folding prediction database published by DeepMind in 2021 accelerated scientific research in fields such as drug discovery but also demonstrated potential for misuse, highlighting the importance of stronger guard rails and AI governance.
links.why: A UK working paper to the 2025 Meeting of States Parties of the Biological Weapons Convention that names AlphaFold in its timeline of life-science advances.

links.siblingText: The UK screening guidance states that increased access to synthetic nucleic acids, coupled with developments in converging tools and technologies such as AI and an increase in knowledge and expertise, may exacerbate the risks of engineering biology.
links.why: The UK synthetic nucleic acid screening guidance (October 2024) names AI among converging tools and technologies in its background statement.
